task_row_model.query: Compute all eigenvalues and corresponding normalized eigenvectors of the n×n tridiagonal Toeplitz matrix T_n with 2 on the diagonal and −1 on the super- and sub-diagonals (entries T_{ii}=2, T_{i,i+1}=T_{i+1,i}=-1). Give explicit closed-form formulas in terms of n and k and indicate the normalization.

documents.content: One standard approach to the spectrum of a tridiagonal Toeplitz matrix is to study its characteristic polynomial p_n(λ)=det(T_n−λI). For the matrix with 2 on the diagonal and −1 on the off-diagonals, the determinants satisfy a recurrence p_k(λ)=(2−λ)p_{k−1}(λ)−p_{k−2}(λ) with p_0=1, p_1=2−λ. This recurrence is equivalent to a shifted Chebyshev relation: p_k(λ)=U_k(x) up to a change of variable x=(2−λ)/2. Roots of p_n(λ) give eigenvalues, and the recurrence can be used to localize and numerically compute them, though an explicit closed-form root formula is not developed here.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarizes the characteristic polynomial recurrence and its relation to Chebyshev polynomials; identifies that eigenvalues are roots but does not produce closed-form expressions.

documents.content: Gershgorin's theorem yields simple bounds for eigenvalues of banded matrices. For each row of T_n the diagonal entry is 2 and the sum of absolute off-diagonals is at most 2 (interior rows) or 1 (end rows), so the Gershgorin discs show the spectrum lies within the interval [0,4] (union of discs centered at 2). These bounds are useful to constrain iterative solvers and to guarantee positive definiteness, but they do not give explicit eigenvalues or eigenvectors; tighter analytic expressions require exploiting structure beyond disc estimates.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides a high-level application of Gershgorin discs to bound the spectrum to [0,4] but does not supply explicit eigenpairs.

documents.content: The matrix T_n has explicit eigenpairs: for k=1,...,n the eigenvalue is λ_k = 2 − 2 cos(kπ/(n+1)). Corresponding eigenvectors v^{(k)} have components v^{(k)}_j = sin(j k π/(n+1)) for j=1,...,n. These satisfy the interior recurrence −v_{j−1}+2v_j−v_{j+1}=λ_k v_j and the boundary conditions v_0=v_{n+1}=0. To normalize, note ∑_{j=1}^n sin^2(j k π/(n+1))=(n+1)/2, so the normalized eigenvector is u^{(k)} with components u^{(k)}_j = sqrt(2/(n+1))·sin(j k π/(n+1)).
documents.reasoning_trace: Gives the closed-form eigenvalues λ_k = 2−2cos(kπ/(n+1)) and normalized eigenvectors u_j = sqrt(2/(n+1)) sin(jkπ/(n+1)), and states the normalization identity used.

documents.content: For solving linear systems with tridiagonal matrices one frequently uses the Thomas algorithm, an LU-type factorization specialized to three diagonals. The method performs a forward elimination to produce modified coefficients and then a backward substitution, yielding an O(n) direct solver with minimal storage. Stability considerations require nonzero pivots; for diagonally dominant or symmetric positive-definite tridiagonal matrices the method behaves well. This exposition focuses on solving T_n x=b efficiently rather than on diagonalizing T_n or finding closed-form eigenpairs.
documents.reasoning_trace: Describes the Thomas algorithm and practical solution of tridiagonal linear systems; does not address explicit eigenvalue formulas or eigenvectors.

documents.content: Iterative eigenvalue methods such as the power method and inverse iteration are commonly used to extract extreme eigenvalues of symmetric matrices. The power method converges to the dominant eigenvector if the spectral gap is nonzero; shifts and inverse iteration can target interior eigenvalues. For symmetric tridiagonal problems, Rayleigh quotient iteration often converges cubically near an eigenpair. These algorithmic techniques analyze convergence and complexity rather than producing closed-form analytic expressions for all eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarizes iterative algorithms (power method, inverse iteration, Rayleigh quotient) for computing eigenvalues numerically; does not provide analytic closed-form eigenpairs.
